findings.finding: SBI extension IDs for TIME (0x54494D45), IPI (0x735049), RFNC (0x52464E43), HSM (0x48534D), and SRST (0x53525354) are defined, but the SBI SSE extension ID and the UNKNOWN_NMI event ID (0xffff8001) are entirely absent. No SBI_EXT_SSE constant exists anywhere in the FreeBSD source tree, meaning the kernel has zero awareness of the SSE extension.

sbi_init() probes TIME, IPI, RFNC, and SRST extensions at boot via sbi_probe_extension(). No probe for the SSE extension. This is currently correct behavior since the kernel does not implement SSE support — probing a service you don't use would be unnecessary. However, if SSE support is added, an SSE probe must be added here.

When active_irq (scause & SCAUSE_CODE) >= INTC_NIRQS (16), the function returns FILTER_HANDLED without any logging. Any S-mode interrupt delivered via a non-standard scause code (>=16) is silently discarded. If firmware delivers an SSE event/NMI via a non-standard interrupt code, the kernel has zero visibility. However, this is also legitimate behavior under the current architecture since RISC-V S-mode only defines 12 standard interrupt codes (0–11 for software/timer/external x user/supervisor/hypervisor/machine). The use of codes 12–15 and >=16 for SSE events is undefined in the base privileged spec.

spec_citations.excerpt: RISC-V S-mode defines standard interrupt codes: 1 (supervisor software), 5 (supervisor timer), 9 (supervisor external). Codes >= 16 are not allocated for standard S-mode interrupts.

findings.finding: The default case in the kernel exception handler calls panic('Unknown kernel exception %#lx trap value %#lx'). If an SSE event is delivered as an exception with an unrecognized scause code (e.g., a non-standard exception code used by the SSE mechanism), the host kernel panics — creating a Denial-of-Service vector: a firmware-initiated NMI event could crash the kernel.

Same panic-on-unknown pattern for user-mode exceptions: panic('Unknown userland exception %#lx, trap value %#lx'). An unknown exception code delivered to a user process context would trigger a full kernel panic rather than delivering a signal to the process.

All interrupts are uniformly dispatched through intr_irq_handler(frame, INTR_ROOT_IRQ). No NMI-specific dispatch path exists. This is architecturally correct for the current codebase: the base RISC-V privileged architecture does not define an NMI delivery mechanism in S-mode (RNMI is M-mode only via the Smrnmi extension). SSE-based NMI delivery to S-mode is defined by the separate SBI SSE specification, which FreeBSD does not implement.

spec_citations.excerpt: The base machine-level architecture supports only unresumable non-maskable interrupts (UNMIs), where the NMI jumps to a handler in machine mode. The Smrnmi extension adds support for resumable non-maskable interrupts (RNMIs) to RISC-V, adding four new CSRs (mnepc, mncause, mnstatus, and mnscratch) and the MNRET instruction — all M-mode only.

findings.finding: Same uniform interrupt dispatch in the user-trap path: intr_irq_handler(frame, INTR_ROOT_IRQ). This is architecturally consistent with the current baseline. No ability to distinguish NMI from regular interrupts exists because the base RISC-V privileged architecture does not define a user-mode NMI path.

vmm_sbi_ecall() handles only three SBI extensions in-kernel (RFNC, TIME, IPI). SBI_EXT_ID_BASE — which includes SBI_BASE_PROBE_EXTENSION used by guests to discover firmware capabilities — falls through to the default case and returns false, forwarding to userspace as VM_EXITCODE_ECALL. This means a guest probing for SSE support via SBI_BASE_PROBE_EXTENSION would receive whatever answer bhyve userspace provides, not what the actual firmware supports. This creates a trust-boundary issue where userspace could incorrectly report SSE as supported.

Unknown SBI extension IDs return false with the comment 'Return to handle in userspace.' If bhyve userspace does not implement SSE handling, a guest's SSE registration or event-handling SBI calls would receive an undefined response. This is the kernel side of a delegation chain where the kernel abdicates responsibility but has no way to audit what userspace does.

When vmm_sbi_ecall() returns false for unhandled SBI calls, the ECALL arguments are forwarded to userspace via vme->u.ecall.args[] and the VM exits with VM_EXITCODE_ECALL. This is the architectural design for extending SBI handling into userspace. The mechanism is correct; the risk is at the userspace layer.

vmmops_exception() returns ENOSYS with the comment 'TODO: implement me.' Exception injection into guests is completely unimplemented. Even if the host kernel could receive an SSE NMI event, there is no mechanism to inject it into a guest vCPU. This is the fundamental blocker for any NMI/SSE virtualization.

The has_exception flag is checked and cleared on every VCPU loop iteration, but the TODO block for exception injection is empty — the flag is silently consumed with no action taken. Any pending exception or NMI event would be silently dropped, with no logging and no delivery to the guest.

VM_INTINFO_NMI is defined as (2 << 8) alongside VM_INTINFO_HWINTR and VM_INTINFO_HWEXCEPTION, following the Intel VT-x/AMD-V intinfo format. However, this constant is unreferenced anywhere in the kernel source tree — it exists as dead code with no consumers. It was likely forward-ported from x86 but never wired into the RISC-V VMM interrupt injection path.

Unknown guest exit reasons (scause values) print the scause via printf and exit with VM_EXITCODE_BOGUS. If an SSE event propagated through the hypervisor trap path as an unrecognized guest trap, the guest VM would see a BOGUS exit rather than a structured NMI delivery. The current printf-based error handling provides no structured error recovery path.

The IRQ type enum defines exactly 12 interrupt types: SOFTWARE/TIMER/EXTERNAL x USER/SUPERVISOR/HYPERVISOR/MACHINE (indices 0–11). This is correct per the RISC-V privileged specification, which defines exactly these 12 standard interrupt cause codes. No room for an SSE/NMI-specific interrupt type exists because the base privileged architecture doesn't define one.

Only INTR_ROOT_COUNT=1 root interrupt controller exists (INTR_ROOT_IRQ=0). All interrupts funnel through a single root. This matches the current RISC-V architecture where S-mode has a single interrupt dispatch path. A separate NMI root was never designed because RNMI is M-mode only and SSE events use a different delivery mechanism.

If intr_isrc_dispatch() fails for a recognized IRQ code (0–15), the code prints 'Stray irq %lu disabled' and permanently disables the interrupt via intc_disable_intr(). An intermittent or transient SSE event arriving on a known IRQ code could trigger permanent disabling of that interrupt line, with no mechanism for automatic re-enablement. This is the standard FreeBSD 'stray IRQ' handling pattern, but it interacts poorly with events that may be delivered transiently.

aplic_intr() claims and dispatches all pending interrupts in a loop via aplic_irq_dispatch(). There is no priority-based categorization or NMI/distinguished-event awareness. For the current architecture this is correct behavior: APLIC delivers standard external interrupts and the kernel dispatches them uniformly.
Same flat dispatch pattern as APLIC. plic_intr() claims and dispatches all pending interrupts without priority or category awareness. This is architecturally correct for the current codebase.
